The thing is, I too was leaning toward dividends as I was starting investing years ago...but the more I learnt how to manage selling, the more I realized I shouldn't be bothered by dividends. It's nice, but a bit irrelevant. A total return strategy makes me enjoy the dividend the index fund spits but I can sell 2% or 4% more as I want. Once you really understand the mechanic of selling, dividends really become meaningless. If your fund makes 17% this year and you sold 4% and got 2% dividends...you withdrew 6%, on a good year that's ok, you keep some of the cash or you spend it whatever. But your portfolio still grew 11%. Just picture an old and mature portfolio not even 30 years just 15 years...We're on August 2026...a -15% correction would bring you back only to February. -50% would bring you to 2023. If selling shares is so much hated, I suspect it's because people are still in the early growing phase, they have never sat on large old gains.

I'm 32 years old and as of this writing. I currently have 3 stocks parked in my Canadian Tax Free Savings Account (TFSA) and 2 stocks parked in my retirement account. It is called the Registered Retirement Savings Plan (RRSP). I am focusing on mostly growth as of right now and will eventually switch to income when necessary. 

For those who are curious about the accounts I mentioned.

The TFSA is great for dividends and long term growth as you can receive dividends, interest and withdraw gains tax free. The downside is you're contributions are limited per calander year; waiting for the next calendar year for your contribution limit to reset after a withdrawl. You do get a yearly increase for the account though. Example for when you turn 18. If you start with $5000 for that year. The next year, the Government will announce an annual increase. Somewhere between $5000-$6500. You add that on top of your previous contributions and you'd have a total of $10000-$11500 that you could contribute to and start your investment journey with. It'll continue to increase each year. However be careful with going over its limit as the government will penalize you 1% per month until you withdraw the overage.

The RRSP on the other hand is designed for long term investing, and will eventually turn into a Registered Retirement Income Fund (RRIF) the downside the RRSP is, early withdrawls are taxable, and you get hit heavily when you withdraw for retirement. Staying a lower tax bracket is wise and the reason you get hit so hard come retirement is because, you can write off your RRSP contributions during tax season. 

Hopefully this info helps!
I am also not a financial advisor. Just someone who was curious about the different accounts that we have in Canada.
